When God’s holy Providence <term>Providence: the protective care of God as a spiritual power guiding human destiny</term> five years ago saw fit to suddenly cast me onto a long and painful sickbed in a foreign city at the beginning of a journey—where I experienced the power of our religion within myself (and for this I wish to thank Him yet among the glorified! <note>The "glorified" or "transfigured" refers to those in the presence of God in the afterlife.</note>), and where, amidst quiet reflections on the world and human life, the most pious resolutions were pressed deep into my soul—I occupied myself, as peace and cheerfulness returned along with the hope for life, particularly with the Bible. # Introduction.

It will forever be proof of the highest wisdom, a test of the sublime esteem for all people—even the most limited—before God, and an undeniable advantage of the Christian book of religion over all others in the world; it will forever be an institution that will be preserved through all changes in ways of thinking, philosophy, and education in all centuries yet to come; it will forever be a model worthy of imitation for everyone who is called to the great business of transferring religious truths into other souls—that the greatest part of our Bible is history. 

In a moderately sized book, there is more narrative, more variety, and diversity than in twenty chronicles. The Bible instructs all people, it portrays all people, and uses the colors of life and truth; it warns all people, it comforts all people. There is no situation into which anyone in this lower world <note>Referring to the earthly, mortal realm as opposed to the divine.</note> can come for which it has no guidance, and no pain for which it has no balm. It contains the whole of human life with all its scenes. 

The religion of the ancient peoples was more about legislation and <term>social regulation<gloss>Original: "Polizey." In the 18th century, this term referred to the general administration, policy, and "policing" of a well-ordered community rather than just modern law enforcement.</gloss></term> than a moral teaching for the heart. The Bible occupies itself more with the human being, with virtue, and with failings in the <term>spiritual state<gloss>Original: "Geisterstaat." This term refers to the community of souls or the moral/intellectual universe under God’s rule.</gloss></term>, than with the best and most excellent institutions of civil society, commerce, or other things in the physical world. # Introduction.

...of inaudible harmonies of the spheres, of <term>cosmogonies<gloss>Theories concerning the origin and evolution of the universe.</gloss></term>, of the spiritual beauty of virtue, of ideal worlds or <term>Platonic republics<gloss>Reference to Plato’s "Republic," symbolizing idealized and often impractical political systems.</gloss></term>, of many spirits and demigods, of merging with the deity, of <term>world-souls<gloss>The concept of an animating spirit or "Anima Mundi" that permeates all nature.</gloss></term>, or other things that are quite insignificant for us citizens of Earth because they lie beyond our horizon. Such things cannot be examined, absorbed, or used by our understanding at all; and even if they were included within the realm of human knowledge, they would still have no moral influence—or only the most remote kind—upon the lowest class of people. These are the people who must work more with their hands than they have time or opportunity to cultivate the mind and tune the heart to the finest and most correct sensitivity—and is this not always, as it ever was and will be, the vast majority of mankind? 

Instead of these lofty riddles, which often even those who taught them did not understand—instead of these phantoms wrapped in turgid, mystical language—which, as all history teaches, effect no true lasting improvement among any people, do not stem the ever-strengthening current of decay in the <term>national character<gloss>The collective moral and cultural identity of a people.</gloss></term>, heal no diseases of the state, do not restrain tyrants, do not deter holy fraudsters, do not tame rebels, neither assert nor strengthen natural feelings in the breasts of fathers and mothers, do not maintain the authority of the voice of conscience, and could not even protect the rights of humanity—

instead of this shimmering false wisdom, with which the deceitful authors of fabricated divine revelations undoubtedly wished to give themselves the appearance of a profound insight that was unfathomable to the rest of mankind, however much it...

# On the Bible in General.

...[could not fulfill what] nature feels and the heart desires: that when God wishes to communicate with His lower creatures, He should take into consideration our moral needs, our errors, prejudices, passions, joys, labors, tears, changes, and partings—our entire improvement and peace of mind. He should not constantly present supernatural subjects in incomprehensible words and turgid imagery, which initially have no effect other than making the thought of God—in which there is always much that is terrifying for the unreformed human—even more unpleasant, and repelling the timid heart. 

Instead, our divine Bible teaches a wise, good, gentle, and humane <term>disposition<gloss>German: "Gesinnung." This refers to a person's underlying moral character or internal mindset.</gloss></term> on a coronation day, on the day of the most pleasant and charming union <note>A reference to a wedding or marriage.</note>, at the grave of a beloved child, in the possession of the greatest riches, under the scourge of the harshest fate, in a dungeon unvisited by the sun—under all possible circumstances, whether pleasant or unpleasant, great, mediocre, or lowly. 

And all of this is clothed in history—just as a physician mixes bitter medicines with sweet things, thereby deceiving the patient’s aversion and achieving his purpose. The Bible is inexhaustible in its descriptions, narratives, biographies, small family portraits, and great, far-reaching revolutions in entire states. It sweeps its readers from one scene to another; the reader is always seeing, yet hears almost nothing <note>The author implies that the Bible "shows" rather than "tells," using vivid imagery instead of abstract lecturing.</note>; the reflection on means and ends, on causes and connections, is left to the reader himself. # Introduction.

...future transformation and change; through all periods of the human race, through all its disfigurements, chastisements, improvements, and elevations—from the third human, who already became a fratricide <note>A reference to Cain, the son of Adam and Eve, who killed his brother Abel.</note>, to the one who could calmly say: "I will soon be sacrificed for my brothers; why are you weeping and breaking my heart? <note>A reference to the Apostle Paul in Acts 21:13.</note> I have learned to be content in all circumstances." <note>A reference to Philippians 4:11.</note> 

Is it not true that for this very reason, even the simplest, most inexperienced, and roughest peasant—or the woman who does not know and would not believe that a mass of new printed books is published every six months—can still read God’s word with pleasure? They remember some of it, understand most of it, and, almost without guidance—or at least guided nearly always correctly by their own feelings—can make immediate applications to themselves, their occupations, and their trade with fields and livestock. They can just as easily apply it to their King, to public institutions, and especially to their own sufferings. 

One must sometimes hear this for oneself to be truly convinced. In doing so, one feels a sweet delight—which must turn into gratitude toward the universal Father of Mankind—to see how strikingly often poor, sick, and plagued country folk apply the stories and passages of the Bible to themselves! 

Who does not enjoy hearing a story? Who does not like to learn what the world of the past looked like? It is pleasant to go back to an age that has long since ceased to exist. We feel a certain sweetness in standing upon the dust of others, and we imagine ourselves greater because we were born after them and can act as judges over the arrangements, customs, deeds, and undertakings of our ancestors. Do not all souls open themselves to history, because it serves to satisfy...

# On the Bible in General.

...of curiosity has an inexhaustible treasure that grows every day? Does not natural history attract all people—young and old, kings, princes, and subjects—because nature constantly shows new, noteworthy sides? Through its infinite artistry, nature multiplies everything; it is great and beneficial in all its arrangements, magnificent in its depiction, and leads our soul to the most pleasant enjoyment by guiding us through countless shades and gradations, from this small earthly globe to the very threshold of God's throne. 

Do we not see it in our children—and they are, as Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), a Roman statesman and philosopher.</note> says, *images of nature*! <note>original Latin: *simulacra naturae*</note>—that, despite their lovely liveliness and cheerfulness, they enjoy going to their grandfather because he can tell them little stories and entertain them? Do we not see it in every religious assembly, that everyone becomes quiet and attentive as soon as the teacher drops the usual tone of lecturing and begins to narrate, lingering on individual events? 

Was that not the magnificent masterpiece of our great predecessor <note>This likely refers to Jesus, whose teaching through parables is highlighted here as a model of effective communication.</note>, through which he earned love and respect even among the most sluggish of the common people? He constantly blended fine, beautiful, natural, and striking stories into his teaching, and taught truths while appearing only to be a painter of human life. Is it not the best way to accustom the delicate souls of children to the softest, sharpest moral feelings, and to keep them constantly attentive, when one tells them fables of people, animals, and plants? They remember these without effort, through laughter and play; and at the end of the clever description, they find the lesson—which is disguised in this garment—almost by themselves, and must acknowledge its value.

It introduces its characters as speaking persons; it gilds nothing over; it conceals nothing. It speaks naturally, and thereby holds a mirror before every person in which he cannot fail to recognize his own well-rendered image.

Human failings slightly obscure the beautiful picture of his life, but the great test of his submission, which he endured so excellently, immediately grants it a new luster—there he stood already as a model for the ancient world of the purest obedience toward God, just as his people, after thousands of years, needed only to look upon the Savior to learn submission to God.

## On the Bible in General.

...to the high-spirited youth, whose rushing blood swells every vein, in those dangerous cities where vice offers itself upon the streets—in those moments where it, adorned with every charm and surrounded by the scent of sweet fragrances, falls around his neck—it is a high, divine goal of self-denial, of overcoming, of self-mastery, of the fear of God, and of integrity. The history of David teaches undeniably that it is a burden to live among the great ones of the earth, or to possess a crown and scepter oneself. From the moment he ascended the throne, his life became a long chain of unrest and turmoil. Before then, he was hidden in the countryside in a shepherd’s hut; he saw the sun rise every morning; he competed with other boys in the meadows, throwing pebbles and stones; he ate milk and fruit; he believed that the moon rose at night for his sake and for the sake of his flock; and he cared for nothing except that his father and brothers were satisfied with his sheep. In this sweet life, which has so much appeal because it is almost entirely nature, without the artificial frame and enclosure of men, he hardly knew that kings existed in the world. ...the side <note>The text continues from the previous page's thought about David's peaceful life in nature.</note>—he awoke to pleasure; whoever saw him kissed the beautiful child with fiery eyes, with blond hair, and with that magnificent red color that Nature herself had placed upon the whiteness of his face, and which, washed in the bright stream, became ever fresher and more beautiful. — With the harp in his hand, shepherds and shepherdesses, animals and birds listened to him in the shadowy thicket; the power of music awakened his natural talent for **poetry** <term>Dichtkunst: The art of composing verse, here suggesting David’s authorship of the Psalms.</term>. But peace, innocence, and the happy simplicity of this blissful life fled far away from him as soon as he had to wield the **scepter** instead of the **shepherd’s staff**. Thrust into the great world, his needs increased every day; and when all were satisfied, he still did not have what he had always possessed as a shepherd in the countryside: an open, cheerful, calm soul. Following the eternal wanting, longing, and striving came a black army of cares, dogging him everywhere like a shadow follows a body. The **passions**, which had previously slept—or, when they broke out, pounced upon small, harmless things and, satisfied with their light prey, lay down again to rest—now became ever more impetuous and violent; they took root, demanded constantly, raged in his breast, and now ruled over him instead of being ruled themselves.

Sleep, which used to visit him under every tree and by every murmuring stream, to which every bird had formerly sung him to rest, was now interrupted by a thousand plans and schemes that his imagination devised and then destroyed. — He soon lost...

->### Introduction.<-

Solomon’s Judgment—which the Bible recounts so briefly and without embellishment—plainly proves that the greatest wisdom is the study of nature and the human heart. Cold, argumentative philosophers could debate quite learnedly whether it would be better to take the child’s life in an instant, or perhaps to see it live for many more years in the arms of a false, wicked mother. But that is no investigation for a mother’s heart. Solomon knew that a true mother would sooner surrender her rights than watch the violent division of her own flesh and blood <note>original: "Leibesfrucht," literally "fruit of the womb."</note> with her tender heart—and that the other woman might be crude enough to accept half a child rather than confess a lie before the King and allow herself to be punished for it.

In those days, the King himself sat in judgment and settled all disputes with common sense and feeling. No thick law book had yet absorbed the legal maneuvering <term>chicanery (original: "Chikane") | The use of clever but misleading talk or legal trickery to deceive.</term>, nor hidden right and wrong in such incomprehensible layers that, amidst eternal bickering and hair-splitting qualifications of the case, the disagreeing parties themselves finally no longer know why the legal dispute began. But because of this, our modern judges also lose that invaluable, human pleasure of witnessing the outburst of nature and recognizing right and wrong by its own language and its peculiar signs. \*)

Solomon’s judgment, of course, only holds true for a time and among a people where there are not yet mothers who are ashamed of being wet-nur— <note>The text breaks off mid-word "Säugam[men]" (wet-nurses).</note>

Through this composition, the poet distinguishes himself from the historian, who must dwell on every single event and honor faithfulness in narration as his primary law. ...passes judgment on the sick man <note>Job</note>, accusing him of conceit and self-importance, and unreservedly blaming him for what any honest man can least tolerate: hypocrisy and dishonesty. Thus follows the description of God's omniscience, against which the deceiver has no mask. The section of the sick man's speeches that follows is a detailed description of the sovereign freedom and supreme power of God in the distribution of His goods. The innocent man, he says, is often swallowed up by the powerful, just as the dove is eaten by the bird of prey, or as the bones of a lamb lie scattered around a wolf’s den (Ch. XII. 1–10). *)

Without limit, and only according to His own highest purposes, God distributes fertility and poverty within creation, and among peoples, He metes out rulers and anarchies, religion and ignorance; He raises up and overthrows nations. This is the teaching of the oldest folk songs, a magnificent piece of which is inserted here (Ch. XII. 11–25). It is a side-glance the sick man casts at his friends, as if they themselves were fortunate but unworthy men (Ch. XIII. 1–13).

# Outline of the Book.

Zophar (Chapter 20) repeats what has already been stated many times, and it seems as though he wishes to tear away even the last hope from the sick man <note>The author frequently refers to Job as "the sick man" to emphasize his physical suffering during the debate.</note> of being happy in other regions of the world (Verses 11, 17). How fertile the poet's imagination must be to always find new traits, new expressions, and new arrangements for such frequent repetitions! Just as Job's character had grown in Chapter 19, when he solemnly appealed to God, the poet now lets a friend step forward who speaks more harshly and strictly with him than those before.

Our author almost surpasses himself (in Chapter 21). He paints and instructs, and the truths and his embellishments are in accordance with experience and nature. What we are told in Psalm 37 and Psalm 73 is also preached by this excellent section. Job begs his friends for silence and tells them once more his philosophy concerning God's providence <term>Haushaltung Gottes: literally "the household of God," referring to the way God governs and manages the affairs of the world</term> in the world. 

The first observation: Many an unworthy person enjoys the advantages and joys of this life until the end (Verses 7–15). 

The second: Some are suddenly snatched away, and God punishes every wrong, often even through their children (Verses 16–21). 

The third: In vain do we raise doubts and questions about this divine allowance. We know nothing, except that He lets it happen (Verses 22–26). 

The fourth: He who asserts the first point does not, for that reason, deny the punishment of the godless. For even he who leaves the world in splendor and abundance is carried toward God's retributions <note>original: "Ahndungen" — in this context, it refers to the inevitable divine justice or consequences that follow a person even into the grave.</note> with solemn pomp at his burial (Verses 27, 30, 34).

Even more forcefully and eloquently than his dishonest opponents, he describes the shameful deeds of many people (Chapter 24), but he also accompanies them when they cross over into that world <note>Referring to the afterlife</note> and are punished (Verses 18–24), and rightfully draws the conclusion from this (Verse 25) that his system <note>Job's theological argument that the wicked do not always suffer immediately on earth</note> neither paves the way for wickedness nor sets limits on eternal justice.

Bildad, who answers him, cannot refute this opinion either; meanwhile, so that it does not appear as if all contradictors have now been overcome, he interjects something (Chapter 25) about the greatness of God and reminds his friend of the general guilt of all people before God, doubtless with the intention of advising him that he should rather suffer injustice than rebel against God, as if He—and not they—had done it <note>Suggesting Job should accept his suffering as a general human condition rather than questioning God's specific justice toward him</note>. The sick man <note>Job</note> immediately tells him how little all of this belongs to the current dispute (Chapter 26, Verses 1–4), and the poet makes use of the opportunity given by Bildad to naturally insert a majestic description of God's greatness, of the boundless scope of His monarchy <term>Monarchie: here used to describe God’s absolute sovereignty and rule over the entire universe</term> and His sphere of activity.

Meanwhile, the short-sighted men finally fall silent, and the unfortunate man uses the peace he is granted to pour out his heart once more. The poet allows him to continue speaking for a long time, occasionally stopping as if to gather his strength again or to wait and see if anyone would still contradict him. First, he gives a repeated, measured declaration with earnestness and solemn dignity that he would consider anyone as his enemy who, because of his misfortune, would deny him his innocence and integrity <term>Rechtschaffenheit: a state of being morally upright, just, and honest</term> (Chapter 27, Verses 1–7).

Then again, [there are] healthy, correct principles [serving] as a measure for the happiness of worldly-minded people. — How precious is the one contained in Verses 8, 9, and 10 <note>Referring to Job 27:8-10, which asks what hope the godless have when God takes their soul</note>. But what common sense does not immediately supply them? If we could not for a single minute rightly guide the rudder of the general government of the world <note>The original German "Weltregierung" refers to the concept of Divine Providence or the way God manages the universe.</note>, why then do we always wish to be wiser than Him whose hand has traced the path for world systems and specks of dust?
Do we demand of Him that He conform to our wishes, which are often so absurd and incomprehensible; that He listen to all our whims, which passions suggest to us and imagination gilds; and that in the great design of His work—which He has always made for millennia to come, with eternal, omniscient regard for future nations whose names are yet unknown—He should grant some validity to everything that we—we ephemeral creatures!—dream, demand, hope, and expect? How little we must yet be acquainted with His greatness! Why do we not look into creation, which everywhere bears His image, see His works, gaze at them in wonder, and remain silent? This is the intent of the final part of Job. ### Introduction.

And who then is this divine poet, who could strike his instrument so powerfully, whom the harp obeyed so willingly? One wishes to know him, yet cannot determine it with certainty. Since history fails us, conjecture takes its place. One examines the spirit of the book, the images, the expressions, and its characteristics, and compares the style of Job with the writing style of the other books of the Bible, in order, if possible, to draw a conclusion with some probability: Clearly, the author must have been a man who knows Egypt as well as Arabia; who is familiar with the manners and customs of the Arabs and Edomites <note>Idumeans; the descendants of Esau living in the region south of the Dead Sea.</note>, and with the ancient traditions and customary laws that were common among Abraham’s descendants long before the Law of Moses was given. <meta>This page continues the argument that the author of the Book of Job was intimately familiar with Egypt, using the papyrus plant as evidence. <header>On the Author of the Book.</header>
<sig>E 2</sig>
<meta>be,</meta>

which only grows in Egypt, and whose bark was formerly split into wide sheets with a needle or torn, so that people wrote on it before the invention of linen paper <note>This refers to the transition from papyrus to rag-based paper.</note>, the poet uses as an image of the brief and unstable prosperity of the unrighteous. (Job 8:11–13.) He says of this reed-like plant that it cannot grow unless it is covered with water in the swamp

One hears from the pulpits regarding the Gospel of Luke 17:11 etc. that this disease [leprosy] was supposed to be a prototype <term>Vorbild: a 'type' or prefiguration in biblical theology where an Old Testament event or condition foreshadows a New Testament truth.</term> of natural corruption... But sin was already in the world then; why the need for a prototype? Because the lepers had to bring an offering afterward? The Israelites had to bring offerings for many other things, for every contact with a dead person, etc. Because the priests, and not the doctors, had to judge it? At that time there were no doctors at all in the world. The priest was theologian, jurist, police councilor, economist, general, poet, music expert, etc. Because David in Psalm 51:9 applies phrases about leprosy to the spiritual deliverance from sins? In all languages, corruption, errors, and the follies of the soul are compared to the diseases of the body. Because leprosy had its seat within, completely disfigured the person, and was contagious and fatal, like sin? Since the Jews brought it out of Egypt before they had even enjoyed their special blessings? Since there were already lepers in the camp, Exodus 4:6–8, Numbers 5:1–4? Since Job is said to have had it, yet he is placed in a much earlier time? Since it is well known that every country has its own natural diseases? Furthermore, the New Testament has nowhere declared leprosy to be a type <term>Typus: similar to "Vorbild," a symbolic representation or foreshadowing.</term>.

# Introduction.

All the rest of the word-painting by the author of **Job** is likewise taken from the nature that he had before him; and one must truly be familiar with the natural history of **Egypt** and **Arabia** if one wishes to understand the poet, do him no violence, avoid attributing contrary, false, or foreign thoughts to him, and not overlook any of his beauties. **Blair** <note>Hugh Blair (1718–1800), a Scottish critic famous for his "Lectures on Rhetoric."</note> correctly noted that **Ossian** <note>The narrator of a cycle of epic poems published by James Macpherson, which were immensely popular in the 18th century.</note>, however full of similes he may sometimes be, never presents a single image that would have been foreign or unknown in the land where his praised heroes lived, where his beloveds breathed, moved, and wept, and where his battles took place. If one compares the poets of modern times with the favorites of antiquity in this regard, the advantage certainly falls heavily on the side of the ancients. They did not live as we do, in cities, villages, lecture halls, and studies—one might almost say, imprisoned. They were always in the open, free world of nature. They did not know everything that lay behind their mountains or beyond their rivers. But they knew the scenes peculiar to their own land most precisely, and they spoke of them powerfully and movingly whenever the god of poetry inspired them. They name no animal, no plant, no stream, no mountain, no rock that every member of their people would not also have known. Our poets, very few of whom truly know the nature surrounding them, do not copy nature; they imagine...

This storm comes to **Palestine** from the west, from the Mediterranean Sea, wreaks havoc on **Mount Lebanon**, and finally tears everything down in the **Arabian desert** accompanied by hurricanes; as a result of the thunder and the lightning striking the forest, the beautiful, lively, slender animal, stunned by terror, gives birth too early, stretching and writhing. When they wish to give birth between Easter and Pentecost <note>German: *Ostern und Pfingsten*; this refers to the late spring/early summer season</note>, they seek out a comfortable spot in the meadows or near young forest clearings where they find tender shoots nearby. This ensures that when they must seek food, they do not have to venture far from their beloved young. If there are wolves in the area, whose attacks they might fear, they prefer to place the calf <note>German: *Kalb*—in hunting terminology, a young deer or fawn</note> near the roads, where those predators do not venture. Often, one finds the young deer lying behind a thick bush or even behind a fallen tree. It remains still in this cover until the mother returns. Then it stands up and suckles from the mother’s udder. She is courageous enough to ward off many a fox and, like a horse, kicks out with her hind legs. As soon as the calf glimpses a human from a distance, it cries out loudly; the mother's sharp ear hears this, and she rushes over with heavy steps, making all sorts of turns back and forth simply to lead the dangerous enemy away from her child’s dwelling. \*) Likewise, the hinds employ every possible means to protect the calf from dogs, and would rather let themselves be hunted by them [than lead them to the young].

What our poet further says about the horse (Chapter XXXIX, verses 19–25) likewise <unclear>proves</unclear> that he must have known Egypt. In mountainous Arabia, one could use chariots as little as in the land of the Jews, which likewise has many mountains; but they were well-suited for flat Egypt, just as we still get our best horses today from Hungary and Poland. The horse is not at all suited to a land where there are mountains and valleys everywhere. There, the donkey travels much more securely, and therefore it was used everywhere for riding and carrying loads. The ancient world cultivated the fields solely with the ox, which was presumably spread throughout the whole world by the Phoenicians—the first people to trade on a large scale—as a true service to us all. 43. (Genesis 32:7, 14, 15, 16; Job 1:3.) Abraham receives gifts in Egypt, but according to his lifestyle, there are no horses among them. As a man who wandered the pastures with his herds and did not support himself through agriculture, but solely through livestock breeding, he would have had no use for them. (Genesis 12:16.) Moses travels with his wife and children from Arabia to Egypt, but he has no horses; they all ride on donkeys. (Exodus 4:20.) When Palestine was taken by the Israelites, one finds no mention of horses in the beginning of their history—specifically in that part which borders directly on Arabia. (Joshua 6:21, 9:4.) Thus, it is certain that Arabia cannot be the natural homeland of the horse. The Bible always places the horse in Egypt and gives it to the enemies of God’s people. Therefore, Hosea in Chapter 14:4 has the Jews make a promise in their prayer of repentance: *We will no longer ride upon steeds*, which means they will no longer rely on their alliance with Egypt in times of war. In the list of the great conquests that Moses made among the Midianites (Numbers 31), no mention is made of horses either. When Saul was already king, they still had no horses in Arabia. (1 Chronicles 5:10, 21.) The Canaanites, who lived closer to the sea, had them (Joshua 11:6), but even when horses were captured in war, the Israelites were permitted to keep only the very fewest of them; yet, they were not to be left to the enemies, because one could inflict considerable damage upon them through this loss. They acted, therefore, according to the strict rules of the laws of war, and inflicted a kind of death upon the animals from which they soon had to die. <note>The author is likely referring to the practice of hamstringing (cutting the leg tendons), referred to in biblical texts as "houghing," which disabled warhorses without the need for immediate slaughter.</note> One finds, therefore, in David’s wars, that it is always only the enemies, and especially the Egyptians, who have cavalry. Moses permitted his people to eat four kinds; see Leviticus 11:22. John the Baptist ate locusts in the wilderness, Matthew 3:4. To the great connoisseur of nature, for whom our century mourns <note>A reference to the famous naturalist Carl Linnaeus, who had recently died in 1778</note>, this could not escape notice. *Linnaeus* identifies the passage in *Job* as referring to the *crocodile*. The head is covered with large square scales; on the body sit more than twenty transverse rows of oblong square pieces, through which no weapon can penetrate, and the tail is also set with a double row of scaly, wood-like spikes. One can therefore wound them nowhere else but on the lower surface of the body, where wise Nature has omitted this firm, unyielding covering, because otherwise the abdomen could neither swell during digestion, nor could the womb of the female expand during pregnancy, as must necessarily be the case. # Whether the Book Speaks of Satan?

I am now approaching another investigation that presents much greater difficulties, and which I would pass by in silence, were it not that prejudices and false opinions often hindered the true and proper use of the most worthy things. The question arises: **does the Book of Job speak of Satan?** And what, then, does the writer say about this head of the evil spirits? Among most commentators, the matter is certainly not subject to any doubt. In almost all times, the passage in Chapter I:6–12 and Chapter II:1–7 has been understood as referring to that spiritual being whom we call the **Devil**, and the friends of the <term>doctrine of spirits</term> <note>original: *Geisterlehre*; in this context, it refers to demonology or the study of supernatural beings</note> have always appealed to Chapters IV:18 and XXIII:23 <note>The author likely refers to Job 33:23, which discusses a "mediating angel," as Job 23:23 does not exist; such citations were often used to support theories of a spiritual hierarchy.</note>.

But if one keeps the <term>map</term> <note>original: *Charte*; here meaning the structural plan or internal logic</note> of the book before one's eyes, one will not expect much of that rebellious spirit in the dialogue. The setting, the entire affair, the point of contention, the arguments from both sides, the characters, the occasions for digressions and episodes, the materials for the embellishment and elevation of style—everything is plucked from the midst of human life and has no relationship at all to the invisible creation. But many who concern themselves with the illumination of the Bible are not always accustomed to surveying the whole of an individual book, and do not always judge with enough insight whether an opinion or explanation they have laboriously extracted from individual words can also be reconciled with the plan and purpose of the writer. To this is added that fine, subtle feeling, which, however little

### Whether the book speaks of Satan?

completely darkened the light of reason, blindfolded them, and through illusions and sensual amusements, instilled in them a disgust and aversion toward all reflection, and firmly shackled them in their sad follies. Paul exhorts them to all Christian virtues so that they might put to shame the cunning intrigues of their slanderers. (Compare Verse 11 with 4:27 and **1 Peter 3:16, 4:15–16**.) Then he reminds them that their own sinful desires would cause them a constant struggle. To this, he says, are added the pagan emperors and authorities who wish to force apostasy <note>The abandonment or renunciation of a religious belief.</note>. This is proven by the turns of phrase that Paul uses in **Romans 13:1** and **Ephesians 5:8**. And finally, he mentions the powerful moral (**1 Corinthians 3:1**) seductive wickednesses—doubtless the evil examples and the godless principles of their fellow citizens regarding the vices of lust and drunkenness, which he already wishes to see removed in Verse 6. # Introduction

...[furthermore], <note>The text begins mid-word ("ther"), likely the end of a word like "furthermore" or "likewise" in the original German, continuing the argument that Paul uses the term "Satan" as a descriptor for human behavior.</note> he describes persons of Satan's mindset and Satan's desires by the name of their dark and contemptible predecessor. He does this to express their ugly side and their malicious efforts with a single—and a strong—word, the kind that his fiery spirit loved and easily found. It is well known that in the young Church of the Redeemer, many false teachers, false apostles, Rabbinic brawlers, <term>pseudo-Christians</term> <note>original: "Afterchristen," a derogatory term for those who follow a perverted or false version of Christianity.</note>, hypocrites, traitors, and malicious individuals caused a thousand troubles, griefs, and vexations for this busy man <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul, whose missionary journeys and conflicts are recorded in the New Testament.</note>.

It is well known that these apostles of declining Judaism, these preachers of collapsing idolatry—these profit-seeking and power-hungry people—did not possess a single spark of his noble generosity, of his burning love for humanity, of his praiseworthy industry, of his sublime selflessness, or of his admirable sufficiency and contentment with little. (In this last trait, perhaps no one in seventeen hundred years has come close to him, except for your jewel, O noble German people! Martin Luther in his letters to the <term>Elector</term> <note>The Elector of Saxony, Martin Luther's political protector. The author is drawing a parallel between the struggles and personal character of Paul and Luther.</note>). 

These people even criticized his character—which was blameless before all mortals (Acts of the Apostles 23:1) and inspired awe even in kings (Acts of the Apostles 26:28)—cast suspicion on his reputation, diminished his gifts, and even mocked his physical infirmities wherever they could; they disturbed his peace and devastated the flower garden <note>A metaphor for the newly established Christian communities or "churches."</note> that he had planted with infinite labor. What wonder then, that with the consciousness of his overflowing good heart—while grief walked ever at his side—he looked upon his opponents at every opportunity and presented them in their true form to his disciples? Just as he knew no greater title than: Ambassador of Jesus Christ, so...

...[In this way] <note>The page begins mid-sentence, continuing the description of how the Apostle Paul addressed his opponents.</note> he gave all disguised and overt enemies the name that belonged to them, naming them according to their intentions and undertakings: tools, helpers, servants, messengers, and coworkers of Satan. Of the influence and protection of Jesus Christ, which this man must have enjoyed to the greatest extent? 

Does a prince anywhere send a <term>plenipotentiary</term> <note>A diplomat or representative invested with full power to take independent action.</note> into his land, and then allow a rebel—who has long since received his judgment and awaits execution in prison—to travel after him, and permit him to persecute, resist, revile, and pile up obstacles before that man with all his official orders in hand, and to tear down and destroy all arrangements behind him? 

And this would have been the fate of the Apostle, if we chose to think of Satan <note>That is, a literal demonic being rather than human opposition.</note> in those passages. # Introduction

Those passages that mention the punishing miracles of the Apostles and, at the same time, make mention of Satan, have already been a stumbling block to many. Unquestionably, 1 Corinthians V. 4, 5 is one of the most complete passages. Paul threatens, upon his upcoming arrival in Corinth, to expel the **incestuous man** <note>original: "Blutschänder"; referring to the man disciplined by Paul in 1 Corinthians 5 for a forbidden relationship.</note> from the assembly of Christians and to **hand him over to Satan**. One would have to claim a manifest absurdity if one wanted to understand this according to the letter. The Apostle could not command Satan; he did not stand over him, and Satan would have accepted no command from him. Humans cannot pass into the realm of spirits, cannot influence higher creatures, and angels can perform miracles just as little as we can. They are, like everything besides God, bound to the order of God. Their powers are a part of the general powers of nature. (Therefore, **Habermann's prayers** <note>Johann Habermann (1516–1590) was a famous Lutheran theologian whose prayer book was widely used; the author here critiques the use of these prayers as "magical" protections.</note> against **poltergeists** <note>original: "Poltergeister"; refers to noisy or disruptive spirits in folklore.</note> are superfluous, harmful, and incapable of being heard.) The Apostle could carry out the exclusion from the worship assembly with all his authority, and upon his prayer, God sent—where it was necessary—a painful illness, which was regarded by the first Christians as a punishment because the messenger of Jesus had predicted it and had announced it beforehand with certainty and confidence. This is how all the miracles of the Apostles must be viewed. (See **Mosheim's** <note>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim (1693–1755), an influential Lutheran church historian often cited in Enlightenment-era debates.</note> explanation...)

...The sense is clear. With two kinds of idioms, Paul describes an extremely painful and sensitive suffering: illnesses, false teachers, scattered lies, etc. Perhaps it was truly a suffering that the mourning man hid within himself. That a **deputy of the devil** <note>original: "Abgeordneter des Teufels"; a reference to the "messenger of Satan" mentioned in 2 Corinthians 12:7.</note> actually struck him is something that no rational person would think. The passage gives rise to much more important reflections.

One should not imagine our poem as merely a well-intentioned, edifying conversation between several good friends at the bedside of someone half-despairing. Everything the author of Job says has its most precise relationship to the plan, to his first and final focus; everything must be judged from the perspective of confirming the doctrine of another world; everything depends on the question: Must God always and without exception reveal his justice in this life, or is there yet another state of being, and another world?

...the innermost part of theology. — No human writer, writing with even a modicum of order and preliminary thought, would allow themselves to be explained in the same way that the Bible is often interpreted. # On Job XIX. 25. etc.

Let one remember that the body of the sick man under these circumstances, according to the testimony of the ancients, finally becomes a single boil. The skin develops blue and violet spots and dry cracks; the outermost limbs swell astonishingly; bones and entire limbs fall from the body; the whole form of the person becomes loathsome and terrible; the breath reeks; the hair falls out; and finally, the color turns completely black. When some of the boils burst open, the putrid smell attracts insects and blowflies <note>The author is likely describing a form of "elephantiasis graecorum" or a severe skin condition often associated with the biblical accounts of Job's "sore boils."</note>; these lay their eggs in the wounds, and maggots <note>original: "Raupen" - literally caterpillars, but used here in the historical sense of larvae or maggots.</note> hatch from these eggs and feast on the corrupted fluids of the unfortunate man — (see Chapter VII. 5. etc.) These and other symptoms of the illness can be gathered from the scattered parts of the book.

Job says constantly that, according to human knowledge, there is nothing more for him to expect than death. What is more natural, then, than that he eagerly looks forward to another world? When others wish to embellish the passage and introduce foreign additions, they only increase the difficulties for themselves. It would be best if one refrained from using the word **Redeemer** <term>Erlöser: The Hebrew word is "Go'el," which refers to a "kinsman-redeemer" or legal protector. The author argues that the modern Christian concept of a Savior/Redeemer may distract from the original legal and historical context of Job's plea.</term> here, for it does not entirely express the poet's thought, and the other Christian meaning immediately comes to everyone’s mind. 

In the oldest translations, one does not find much comfort; Doctor Luther took some inaccuracies from the Greek <note>The Septuagint.</note> and from the Latin <note>The Vulgate.</note>. In Verse 26, one will never find a sound, error-free meaning until one changes the punctuation—consulting the Syriac and other ancient versions—as Mr. Michaelis <note>Johann David Michaelis, a 18th-century biblical scholar.</note> has indicated, see <note>original: "Prolegom. p. 44."</note> *Introduction, page 44.* and <note>original: "Velthuysen Exercitatio in Iobi XIX."</note> *Velthuysen's Dissertation on Job 19.* 

In the new English Bible, *The Holy Bible, Cambridge 1775*, the emphasis <note>original: "Nachdruck"</note> of Verse 25 has also been lost, and the thought displaced: *For I know, that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand upon the latter day upon the earth.* The poet never says "to stand over the dust." To "stand over the earth" is, here, far too weak, too vague, and too dull.

# Introduction.

...can be composed from the complaints of Job. This condition has been observed among lepers in America, and German physicians have noted it in a leper in Göttingen. (See J. D. Michaelis, *Notes on Chapter II of Job*, pp. 4–8; and in Linnaeus, *Academic Delights* <note>original: "Amoen. Acad." – a collection of dissertations by Carl Linnaeus</note>, Vol. VII, Dissertation 131, *On Leprosy*, p. 94 etc. See also Fabricius, *Travel to Norway*, Hamburg, octavo, 1779, p. 372 etc.; he found lepers in the St. George's Hospital <note>original: "St. Jurgenshoſpital"</note> in Bergen.)

One type of leprosy is called **elephantiasis**, because the skin turns black and folds together, much like the outer skin (*epidermis*) of the elephant. While the elephant's skin is very thin in some places and attached to the flesh by fibers, in other places it is very thick and its sweat pores are easily clogged, which means the animal certainly cannot remain healthy for long. (See *Memoirs to serve the history of animals*, prepared by Mr. Perrault <note>Claude Perrault, a 17th-century French anatomist and architect</note>, Part III, 1734, quarto, Paris, no. X.) To prevent this, the skin of the elephant in the menagerie at Versailles is constantly rubbed with a sponge dipped in oil; this keeps it dark in color but soft and supple.

Such a skin, such a disease—which unites everything loathsome, repulsive, and painful, drives away sleep or embitters it with anxious dreams, and is constantly accompanied by the danger of suffocation—was what Job endured. Through this, his soul becomes clear; he gathers the final strength of soul and body to express his joy over the impending beautification and glorification of his indescribably ravaged body. In other passages, he had only comforted himself with the idea of immortality; now he speaks with the strongest emotion of the resurrection of the body and expresses a longing desire to see God. There is, therefore, nothing present that would compel us, in this great [passage]...

# On Job 19:25 ff.

The church hymn (*Jesus, My Confidence* <note>original: "Jesus, meine Zuversicht" — a famous 17th-century Lutheran hymn often sung at funerals, which uses Job 19:25–27 as its primary scriptural basis</note>), which was composed based on the words of *Job* with an infusion of New Testament concepts and teachings, has undoubtedly contributed much to making this false interpretation general. Dying righteous people find refreshment in these words, and the life and return of the Redeemer to awaken the dead rests upon the unerring testimony of the *New Testament*. Thus, the matter itself is true, but the passage in *Job* is no proof of it.

And who would be so completely unfamiliar with the arrangement of the Bible that they would not consider a book divine simply because nothing of the *Messiah* is contained within it? Is *Christ’s* so-called Sermon on the Mount (*Matthew 5, 6, 7*) not highly important and instructive for the reason that he does not mention his atoning death by even a single syllable? Is *Paul’s* speech in Athens (*Acts 17*), or the one before Governor *Felix* <note>Marcus Antonius Felix, the Roman procurator of Judea before whom Paul stood trial</note>, any less from the mouth of the Apostle because he likewise does not cite the Redeemer’s death on the cross? Could God make known the core of religion in the earliest times, in the first infancy of the human race, at the beginning of the Church? **In** the land of Uz <note>original: *Uz*</note> *) there once lived Job. He was a worshiper of the true God, and at the same time—out of fear of Him—a virtuous and <term>upright|original: *rechtschafner*, meaning a person of integrity and moral soundness</term> man. ### Chap. III.

Finally, Job broke his silence, cursed his fate, and began:

Unfortunate be the day on which I was born, let the night be cursed that saw the conception of a boy! Oh, that this day without a sun had never been! That God on high had known nothing of it! That light had never risen over it! Thick, deep darkness must reclaim it, blackness dwell over it; oh, that my unfortunate life had scared it back from the horizon! # Translation

...she [the papyrus] does not stand in the swamp? Can this reed grow tall if it is not always in the water? Without water, the plant withers even before the harvest, before it is cut down, sooner than any other grass. And this is also the story of all those who forget God! Every expectation [is destroyed]— <meta>completes the word 'Erwartung' from the catchword 'tung'</meta>

---

...the more artistic poetry of Bildad’s speeches is distinguished. In such songs, the entirety of religious doctrine and the practical wisdom of the human race was once contained. Before man could write, before schools existed, these sublime songs held all authority. Youth learned them by heart, and thereby enriched themselves with the experiences of those who had lived for centuries. In the books of Moses, many such individual pieces and inserted passages occur (see the *Letters on the Mosaic Writings and Philosophy*). Among the Scots and Highlanders, many songs of Ossian <note>A reference to the "Ossian" poems published by James Macpherson in the 1760s, which were celebrated in the 18th century as authentic ancient folk epics.</note> still circulate in praise of heroes, hospitality, etc.

The uncertain fortune of the sinner is compared with the paper-reed <term>Papierstaude: The papyrus plant, used in antiquity to make paper.</term>, regarding which see the author’s introduction above; hereafter it is compared with the light, thin, swaying spider-beams <note>An archaic way of describing the structural threads of a spider's web.</note> upon which the spider robs and murders, and which everyone knows; and finally, the beautiful comparison with the plants occurs which we now call parasitic plants <term>original: *Pl. parasiticae*</term> or ephemeral plants <term>original: *Pl. ephemerae*; plants that live only for a day.</term> in botany. These grow rapidly at first, bursting with sap, and have a very loose, stretchable tissue. They can wind themselves around a garden house in twenty-four hours, striking their roots everywhere, entangling themselves, and drawing the moisture from between the stones. They always proliferate strongly wherever they have once clung, climbing high, and are capable of suffocating all other plants next to them. 

However, in a short time—according to the great law of nature: *What ripens quickly does not last long*—they are destroyed again in a single night by a frost, by too much moisture, by a hot day, by a small displacement, or by the slightest damage from an insect. The Bible does not speak of this elsewhere except here and in Jonah 4:6–7, where no gourd plant is meant, but rather the *Ricinus L.* <term>The castor oil plant (Ricinus communis), which grows rapidly and has large leaves, often identified as the plant that provided shade for the prophet Jonah.</term>

# Job Ch. VIII.

...expectation <note>Completes the word "Erwartung" from the previous page.</note> of the enemy of religion! Everything he defied is trampled to the ground; his hope is like the **spider’s web**. It leans upon its house, and it is itself not firm. It dwells upon it, but it does not last long—the unjust man resembles a plant that is full of sap at the rising of the sun; its branches run quickly over the whole trellis of the garden, the roots take hold everywhere among stones and grasp at walls, and a small, unknown cause injures the plant—so it is gone from its place, as if the spot had never held it, never seen it! See, so uncertain is the pleasure on the path of the godless! But certainly, they always grow forth again from the dust. —Therefore, always think: God protects the pious; to the evildoers He does not offer His hand in their fall. He will yet give you cause for loud laughter; you will yet exult over Him. Your enemies will have to hide themselves in their shame, and the tent of the robbers will finally disappear.

### Chapter X.

Oh, weary of life, I will pour out all my complaint; I will tell of the piercing pain of my soul. Let it be permitted for me to say to God: Do not condemn me, or at least let me know beforehand the specific sins for which you are angry with me! Do you take pleasure in oppressing and casting off your creature? Can you look down upon the schemes of sinners like the rising sun? <note>Job asks if God looks favorably—as the sun does when it rises—upon the plans of the wicked while he suffers.</note> Do you then also have such vengeful eyes as humans have? Do you live only a few days, like humans? A few years, like the sons of the earth? Must you then seek out my sins so precisely, so sharply? You know well that I have not sinned intentionally! That no one can rescue me from your punishments! Your hands formed me; they have joined everything in me with the greatest skill—and now—alas, everything is different! You are destroying me yourself once more! Remember, then, that you yourself—not I—fashioned me as if from clay, and now you want to push me back into the dust! Did I not arise from a few drops, as milk is pressed out? Did you not let me become firm, bit by bit, like curdling cheese? \*) At my first coming into being, you clothed me with skin and flesh, m <note>original: "m" - likely the start of "mit" (with).</note>

# Job Ch. X.

...you equipped me with bones and nerves. Life, and since I have lived, I have received many blessings from you; your oversight always preserved my breath. And these current tragic fates of mine you had already secretly decreed within yourself! Does it suit your creative care to torture me now at the end of my life? Could I have thought back then, when I was still your favorite, that you intended this? Have I somewhere unknowingly sinned terribly, and you do not forget it for me, do not release me from my sin, and I always appear as a guilty party before you—oh, then woe to me! So the illness lasts a long time. ### Job Ch. XII.

Would I then not have noticed if I had spoken untruths? Should not the ear test my words, just as the palate judges the taste of food? You appeal to the songs of the ancestors; so do I. Certainly, old men living through the centuries could gather wisdom; their great age brought ripe understanding. But you know the song of the world of old: in truth, only God has true wisdom and power; He alone has insight and clever— <meta>catchword: cleverness</meta>

—ness spoken. Such distorted <note>original: "schielende" – literally "squinting," implying a biased or warped perspective</note> ideas are countless in the writings of those who wish to lead us to God through nature. But it is inexcusable when he <margin>p. 365.</margin> says: "To a Christian naturalist <note>term: Naturkündiger — a 18th-century term for a scientist or student of the natural world</note>, the earth—however precious, beautiful, or useful it may be—should rightly become distasteful." Oh, my brothers! Not so! Do distinguish between the earth and human society. The latter can sometimes become loathsome to us, but not entirely, because we should always do good (Galatians 6:9; John 9:4; 17:4).

The creation, however, remains forever God’s work and must be the most venerable and pleasant sight to us. It nourishes us always; why then should we give it a dark look? We never learn all the wonders of our earth; we can delight in its beauties every day. The Bible speaks quite differently (Psalm 104; 8; 19). If God denied us all pleasure here below, how could we expect much good from Him in another world? God’s community, the Church of the Redeemer, is indeed on the earth; Wieland <note>Christoph Martin Wieland (1733–1813), a prominent German Enlightenment writer and poet.</note> says (*Sympathies*, p. 26) that God would not tolerate it if He did not find a prevailing goodness in it. All creatures still suffice for their intended purposes; what then shall we do in heaven other than study God’s works and feel their charms? Following the example of Jesus Christ, a heavenly mind does not consist in railing against God’s creation—that would kill all trust, all love, and all gratitude toward God.

Joyful thanks to Count Stolberg <note>Friedrich Leopold zu Stolberg-Stolberg (1750–1819), a poet whose "Hymn to the Earth" celebrated the divinity found in nature.</note> for his *Hymn to the Earth*! published in the *German Museum*, September 1778.

Be so full of dangerous teachings that overturn all religion <note>In this context, 'religion' refers to the established order of piety and fear of God.</note>? # Job Ch. XV.

The heavens are not pure before Him. How much less then a wicked, a corrupt human, <note>One observes here that even the oldest book in the world—and the first portion of the Bible—contains the doctrine of the universal corruption of mankind, expressed in powerful poetic imagery.</note> who refreshes himself with sins as a thirsty man drinks water?

Now, listen to me; I wish to instruct you. I will tell you of my own experiences. Do not be angry at this; the wisest have always declared it without fear, and they know it so certainly that they do not hide it even from their ancestors. I refer to those who still possess their own unique homeland entirely alone, where no stranger has yet trespassed: <note>This means he intends to recite a song from the ancient world, composed in the heart of Arabia among a people proud of their unmixed blood. In the poem itself, a godless man is presented who is just as comfortless and helpless as Job had described himself. First, the poet depicts the tortures of a guilty conscience; then he portrays the debauched sinner who wishes to defy God in heaven; and of this man, he finally says that everything fails him. The Arabian lives from the palm tree, just as we live from grain. Thus, if the dates fail to grow, it is the same as if a harvest were to fail. In the heart of Arabia, there was also a small amount of viticulture, and they raised olive trees in their gardens; but all this fails for the godless man—it does not reach maturity, and even his family dies out.</note>

The godless man trembles as long as he lives; trembling, the enemy of humanity counts the years until death that are still hidden from him. He always hears the approach of misfortune; even in his best state of happiness, the fear of ruin overcomes him. He must not hope that his misfortune will ever cease. David began a terrible war with the Ammonites because they had cut off the beards of his messengers. 2 Samuel 10:4–5. ### Job Ch. XX.

...[water] channels, those streams and canals of honey and milk in paradise! <note>*) See the detailed geographical and cultural note below regarding these metaphors of abundance.</note> The wages of labor must
<meta>catchword: he</meta>

In the Orient, poisonous snakes are more common than they are here. One must not think of dragons; they exist nowhere except in the imagination of idle people. It is impossible to determine which species of snake the poet intended, and it is also unnecessary. Luther translates word for word: *the tongue of snakes*; however, the poet speaks the language of the common people, who judge by appearances. The tongue of snakes does not bite and does not sting; but, before the snake strikes with its hollow, movable venom-teeth <note>original: *Tela f. Arma*, meaning "weapons" or "tools of war"</note>, it thrusts out its forked tongue and prepares to bite. This is why the tongue was traditionally mistaken for the instrument of poisoning.

\*) Since water is so rare in Arabia that their geographers mark the locations of springs on maps, a garden flowed through by a river—which consequently has many divisions, pipes, and channels—is for them the most pleasant of all places; this is how they imagine Paradise. Muhammad in the Koran speaks so often of the streams in Paradise that it becomes tedious. In Damascus and Isfahan, everyone must pay for good water, receiving it from an overseer who manages the many pipes and channels. Because the people drink water as their primary beverage, they distinguish carefully between good and bad water (Song of Solomon IV. 12, 15). Regarding the "water of Paradise," the poet says it is like pure milk and honey. A stream of "melted butter" <note>This refers to a common but perhaps literalistic translation of the Hebrew word 'chemah'</note> would be an absurdity—who would find the sight of so much fat pleasant? The ancient Jews did not eat butter, nor did the Arabs; they prepared their food with much purer and tastier olive oil, or <term>tree oil <note>original: "Baumöl"; an older term for high-quality vegetable or olive oil</note></term>. In all these scriptural passages, the word actually refers to thick, sour, refreshing milk from sheep, camels, or cows. (Genesis XVIII. 7, 8; Judges IV. 19, V. 25; Proverbs XXX. 33; Isaiah VII. 15, 16, 22; and Job XXIX. 6). The travelers Arvieux and Shaw found this lifestyle of drinking a great deal of milk—much like in Switzerland—also

—of his years? <note>This completes the sentence from the previous page: "And what does he care for his children after death, when the lot [decides] the number of his years?"</note> Does one among you wish to teach God wisdom? ### Chapter XXV.

Now Bildad the Shuhite <note>One of Job's three friends who came to comfort him, though his "comfort" often took the form of harsh judgment</note> interrupted: His dominion is fearsome; beware of Him, for in His heights He surely holds judgment. The onyx is a type of fine silica, which has the closest relationship to the chalcedony; it is mostly transparent with many colored veins and threads drawn through one another. The ancients carved many vessels from it, and if the artist had skillfully followed the various veins, such a figure had a great effect on the eye. The famous Mantuan vessel <note>The *Vaso Mantovano*, a renowned ancient Roman vessel carved from a single piece of sardonyx, depicting agricultural rituals.</note> is a six-inch onyx; there are twelve figures on it, and the entire piece depicts a festival of Ceres <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture.</note> and Bacchus <note>The Roman god of wine.</note>. (See *Neueste Mannigfaltigkeiten* <note>A contemporary 18th-century German periodical titled "Latest Varieties."</note> Vol. II, p. 211 etc.) The sapphire is the sky-blue gemstone that often appears in jewelry and natural history collections, though its natural classification <note>original: "N. *) To understand these idioms, one must again recall the symptoms of the disease that I described in Chapter XVI. The highly corrupted scorbutic <note>original: *skorbutische*. Refers to symptoms resembling scurvy, which 18th-century scholars often used to categorize Job's various skin and bone afflictions.</note> blood necessarily causes a violent, unbearable irritation in the membrane (**periosteum**) <note>original: *Periostium*. # Translation

*) The poet presents the genius <note>Here, "genius" refers to the innate spirit or driving intellectual force of a person</note> of man, of which Elihu is quite proud, as a breath or wind that fills his chest and his whole body, expanding like young or fermenting wine, and would rather tear everything apart than be enclosed in a narrow space. # Job Ch. XXXIII.

### Chapter XXXIII.

Hear then, Job, my speech; mark all my words. I have opened my mouth, and my tongue speaks. What I think in my heart, and all that I know, I wish to say; I will present chosen things. God’s breath created me; the breath of the Almighty is within me. Refute me if you can; set yourself against me for the struggle. Before God, I am just like you; I, too, was formed from clay. My accusations shall not cast you down. What I charge you with shall not become too heavy for you.

But—this you cannot deny—you said in my hearing, I had to hear this language: "I am pure, without sin, radiant; I cannot be blamed for any injustice. What he finds to criticize in me is a trifle; he views me at once as his enemy; he locks my feet in a block <note>original: "Block" — referring to the stocks, a wooden frame used to restrain the feet of prisoners</note>; he occupies every possible exit with guards." (See Ch. XIII).

Behold, in this you are certainly not right. Let me answer you: God is surely much greater than mortals. Why do you wish to strive with Him, as if demanding that He give you an account of everything He says and does? — God warns people once, perhaps even twice, but after that, not again. *) In a dream, through a vision in the night, when midnight sleep falls upon men and each rests upon his bed, then He opens their ear and terrifies them—

---

*) After a long introduction, the opinion of this man <note>referring to Elihu</note> finally follows, namely: Job has sins of ignorance <term>Unwissenheitssünden: sins committed without conscious intent or full awareness of their gravity</term>. So that these do not become dominant and intentional, God chastens him through illness, etc. Which specific sins are meant to be punished here depends on angels or dreams, etc. See the introduction above regarding the investigation of Satan.

<summary>Elihu begins his formal argument against Job, asserting that God is too great to be questioned and that suffering or nightmares are actually divine warnings intended to steer a person away from accidental sins.</summary>

# Translation

### [Continued from previous page]

...them through His warnings, so that they might turn away from their evil deeds, and He might cover the open pit <note>original: "Grube" — a common biblical metaphor for the grave or the underworld</note>. # Translation

### Chapter XXXVII.

Truly, at this my heart trembles and leaps out of its place. Listen closely to His mighty voice, hear the terrible sound that comes from His mouth. He sends it out under the whole heaven; His lightning reaches the very edges of the earth. After it, the thunder roars again; He thunders with His majestic voice, but no one can track the thunder and lightning on their path; one only hears the sound of the thunder. Incomprehensible is the roar of God’s voice; God’s deeds are too great, we do not understand them. — He commands

Nations have compared the crashing of thunder to the driving of a chariot upon which God sits. According to the poets' imagination, the thunder-cloud or the thunder-chariot is pulled by four living creatures, which Ezekiel calls Cherubim—courageous beasts that must be tamed with a bridle. In the midst of the thunder-cloud, the Oriental <note>original: *Morgenländer*—referring to the cultures of the ancient Near East</note> imagines the throne of God, and God Himself upon it. Around Him is a treasure of flames or a sea of fire; on the outside are thick black clouds, which nonetheless glow with a bright radiance from the fire shining through. Inside is the greatest heat, while outside is the harshest cold. The poet admires the wise arrangements in nature through which fortune and misfortune are distributed in the human world. He portrays it as if God occasionally grasps streams of fire from the glowing lake around Him with both hands, scattering them with fire-red hands across the high heavens as He wills—waving them about seemingly at random, yet precisely marking the path for them and naming the people they are to seek out and consume, or leave in peace. — O you teachers, who have the good fortune to work among common Christians, use this passage to preach to your listeners—who do not fear the thunderstorm because they think it refined or noble to do so—about God's greatness and His loving providence even in the majestic tumult of nature!

On the Coromandel Coast <note>The southeastern coast of the Indian subcontinent</note>, the weather alternates with the Malabar Coast <note>The southwestern coast of India</note>. The former has rain when the latter has the dry season, and vice-versa. During the hot season, the rain flows from the mountains of the West Coast toward the East Coast, benefiting it just as the Nile does for Egypt. When the dams and sluices used to channel this rainwater were once allowed to fall into ruin, a price hike and famine ensued throughout the entire land. (See Pressier's accounts in the *East Indian Reports*, and in the *New Hamburg Magazine* Vol. 93, p. 284.)

<note>This section continues from a previous page, likely discussing the Argali sheep.</note>
-gali, Musmon, or the wild Siberian sheep <note>original Latin: "Ovis fera sibirica"; described by Peter Simon Pallas (1741–1811) in his "Spicilegia Zoologica," a foundational work in zoology</note> [found in] the highest mountains in Tyrol, the Valais, Crete, Asia, etc. It clears the most dangerous heights with astonishing leaps, enjoys the finest herbs, becomes amazingly strong and courageous like a small stag, and always breathes the purest air; all unhealthy vapors are beneath him, and he is often elevated 6,000 feet above the level of the sea. Those who have seen the terrifying leaps that ibexes <term>Steinböcke: Alpine Ibex</term>, chamois <term>Gemsen: a goat-antelope species found in the mountains of Europe</term>, and all alpine animals often make—leaping from a high cliff six fathoms <note>A "Klafter" or fathom was roughly 6 feet; thus, a leap of 36 feet</note> wide, almost vertically down onto a steep rocky peak—marvel at the sharpness of the eye with which they measure the jump so precisely. Otherwise, they would obviously leap to their deaths. They marvel, too, at the skill with which they know how to maintain their balance after such a sudden plunge from above. (See *Travels to Switzerland*, Vol. II, p. 155.) But to how many dangers would the pregnant mothers and the weak young be exposed if the goodness of the Creator did not guide their perilous way and prove great and glorious even on the highest peaks! Naturalists, hunters, and farmers know that the hind <term>Hirschkuh: the female Red Deer</term> carries for nine months, and that the goat gives birth after the sixth month, but who among us can come to the aid of every female in all circumstances? Who teaches them to rid themselves of their burden without support or assistance? Who guides the young in the forest to the succulent herbs? The God who must eternally be our heart's delight and the goal of our most fervent love! See the introduction above.

# Translation

...ed mountains is his pasture; he seeks after every green blade. *)

*) I have already stated in the Introduction regarding the author of the book (p. 78) that one should not think here of a horned donkey, nor of some monstrous beast, but must naturally understand it to be the wild, untamed donkey. The poet regards it as a great arrangement of God in nature that humans were indeed able to force some donkeys and some oxen into servitude, but that from these very same species, individuals remain who are not subjected to the yoke of slavery, and who have preserved their courage, their speed, cheerfulness, and sharpness of senses in the sweet enjoyment of freedom. And even now, one finds in Africa extremely fast and lively wild donkeys, which are very different from our donkeys who are forced into servitude and commonly mistreated. In general, donkeys are playful in their youth, and often quite well-behaved. Donkeys come from Arabia, and even now the Arabian ones are the best. The speed of the wild donkeys in running is so great that only a horse from Barbary <note>The Barb or Berber horse is a North African breed known for its great speed and stamina</note> can keep up with them. They eat the toughest and most unpleasant plants that grow in stagnant waters, in which a portion of the salt—with which the soil in Africa is saturated—is found dissolved. Since time immemorial, donkeys have also been used in the Orient <term>Morgenländer: literally "people of the morning lands," a historical term for the Near East or Levant</term> for riding and for carrying loads. Olearius <note>Adam Olearius (1599–1671) was a German scholar and diplomat known for his detailed travelogues of Persia and Russia</note> says that the donkey drivers have a chain with an awl on their whips, which they rattle constantly, pricking the animal, and they shout incessantly at their pack animals. The poet alludes to this eternal shouting of the driver; for the free donkey, this wretched voice does not constantly ring in his ear. He prefers the happiness of seeking his nourishment on the mountains and skipping about for the sake of every little blade of grass as long as he pleases, over the honor of being ridden by humans and being kept for all sorts of work in the city. (See Buffon's *Natural History of Quadrupeds*, Berlin translation, Vol. I, p. 216 etc. <note>Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon (1707–1788), was a French naturalist whose "Histoire Naturelle" was a foundational work of the Enlightenment</note>). In America, there were originally no donkeys; the Spaniards brought them there...

*) Regarding the choice and explanation of the words that occur in this passage, I have spoken above in the Introduction to Volume I of this book, page 80. Here I must only explain the matters of natural history. The poet admires the activity and the early awakening of birds. A sharp ear, their rapid digestion, and their constant hunger drive them to this. Concerning the wood-grouse <term>Auerhahn: *Tetrao Urogallus* L. (The 'L.' refers to Linnaeus), also known as the Western Capercaillie</term>, it is known that, especially during the mating season <term>Balzzeit: The specific courtship and display period of certain birds</term>, it stands on the trunk of a spruce or fir toward sunrise; quite deafened and blinded by ecstasy, it often begins to call to the female as early as two o'clock in the morning. All birds stir early, but birds of prey in particular often conduct a hunt in the morning twilight before the day has broken, because they must later retreat when the full light blinds their eyes. They leave their nests and yet in most cases do not find the eggs <note>The author likely means that their nests are hidden or protected by the trees, or is contrasting the tree-dwelling birds' specific nesting sites with the ostrich's open sand-nest</note>, because they live in trees. 

But the opposite of all these is the ostrich <term>Strauß: *Struthio Camelus*</term> (see the copperplate engraving in Buffon’s *Natural History of Birds*, Berlin Edition, Vol. III, p. 124 etc. Plate LXXV). This bird of Asia and Africa, which is indisputably the largest among all birds and seems to be more a four-footed animal than a bird, lays between 30 and 50 eggs; the first lies in the center, and the bird lays the others very skillfully in a circle around it. One finds their empty shells everywhere in Europe in cabinets of curiosities and on dining tables. The accounts of their number, size, food, and the laying season vary greatly among travel writers. 

Hardly a fourth part of these eggs hatch. In the sandpile which they scratch together with their feet in order to lay the eggs, they do indeed receive the necessary degree of incubation heat <term>Brutwärme: The warmth required for hatching</term>, and at night the ostriches themselves are said to sit on the eggs and protect them from the cold. However, since the bird in the Sahara Desert must often run about for a long time before it finds food, it does not afterwards find the way back to the nest in this trackless land. Also, the...

It is said that the mother herself even breaks some eggs and feeds the other young with them. The Arabs often gather these eggs and eat them. Often they find fresh and rotten eggs side-by-side, and the hatched and half-dead young wander about, crying piteously for their mother. (see *Shaw’s Travels to the Levant*, p. 388) <note>original: "Shaws Reis. nach der Levante"</note> Clearly, the ostrich does not possess the far-reaching sight, the sharp sense of smell, the fine hearing, the deep affection, or the powerful instincts for the preservation of its kind that other birds have, and which in some nesting hens rise to the point of fury. Its nature is fearful and shy, its power of discernment is weak, its tongue is dull, its appetite insatiable, and its mating instinct is indeed hot, but it also passes quickly; it lacks the marital tenderness and maternal care that we find in other animals. The poet presents this as if God had given him no understanding. The meaning is: he lacks those remarkable instincts through which an animal often approaches the level of a thinking human being more than other creatures do. Nature found this arrangement beneficial, for otherwise ostriches would multiply infinitely and harm the balance between other animals and plants. Yet the species does not die out; one still finds whole armies of ostriches in some regions, and Europe now demands more than ever the feathers of these birds for our head-dresses <term>Kopfputz: elaborate ornamental hair arrangements or hats popular in the 18th century</term>, which are composed of all possible things from all parts of the world. His nature, which shuns humanity, is also clear from Leviticus 11:16, Deuteronomy 14:15, Isaiah 13:21, 34:13, 43:20, and Jeremiah 50:39; and his carelessness toward his young is evident from Lamentations 4:3. But as small as the ostrich...
