### Chapter XL.

And now God spoke further to Job out of the storm, and said:

Gird yourself now like a man; I will question you, and you must give an answer. Do you still wish to overturn my ordinances in the world? To prove me wrong so that you may be in the right? Do you then have an arm like God’s? Can you also thunder with your voice as He does? Adorn yourself then; rise up in your splendor. Clothe yourself in magnificent radiance. Let your wrath flow out like a stream in every direction; look around at all the proud and cast them down. Yes, look upon them all, the rebels, and bow them low; crush every villain in his place. Plunge them all with their faces in the dust; lock them all in hidden dungeons. Then I will also say that you are great, if your own right hand can help you!

Behold the beasts <note>original: *Thiere*; here referring specifically to the great creatures of creation.</note> that I have placed alongside you! The elephant <note>original: *Elephant*; most modern translations identify this creature as the 'Behemoth'—likely a hippopotamus—but 18th and 19th-century commentators often identified it as an elephant.</note> himself eats grass and herbs just like the oxen! Look at his strong loins! And the power of his reproductive organs! Wondrously he swings his trunk <note>original: *Rüssel*; the Hebrew text literally refers to a 'tail,' but the author follows a tradition that interprets the Behemoth as an elephant swinging its trunk like a cedar tree.</note> like a slender cedar; on all sides, his tendons are woven together. His bones are masses of bronze; all his limbs are like iron bars. He stands at the top among the most beautiful animals, and yet his master plays with him. The mountains bear food for him, and all other animals play peacefully beside him. He lies down under shady trees; he hides in the reeds by the swamp. Great trees cast their shadow over him; the willow thickets by the river cover him.

...the lobe, or finger, located at the front [of the trunk], with which it [picks up] small morsels from all types of food and puts them piece by piece into its mouth. Does the crocodile simply lie down the moment it catches sight of a human? He is not even bold enough to wake it up. — How then will he stand before me? Where has anyone first given me something, that I should repay him? What is under all the heavens is mine! I want to tell of what it alone possesses; I want to praise its strength and its subtle cunning. Who has ever uncovered its garment <note>Referring to the crocodile's skin.</note>? Who has ever put a bit in its mouth? Who can tear open its jaws? Terror is all around its teeth! Brazen shields cover its back, so tight, so firmly joined to one another, as if they were sealed together. One lies upon the other, so that not even air can pass through. One shield touches the other, and they are so joined to one another that they cannot be separated. The crocodile awakens as soon as it becomes light; at the break of dawn, it opens its eyes. It is as if burning torches came out of its mouth, as if sparks of fire tore themselves away from it. Steam shoots from its nose, as it rises from a boiling pot, or as the marsh reeds give off vapor.

### Job Ch. XLI.

His snorting kindles coals; one would think bright flames burst from his throat. His neck is the seat of strength, and before him leaps malicious joy <note>The German *Schadenfreude* here suggests a personification of terror or the "leaping" mischief that precedes a predator.</note>. His fearsome limbs cling tightly together, and over him is solid metal <note>A metaphor for the crocodile's exceptionally hard scales.</note> that cannot fall away. His heart is impenetrable, like a piece of rock, firm as the lower millstone. When he rages, all the animals on earth are afraid. *) If one tries to attack him with the sword, nothing is achieved—nothing with spears, lances, or weapons.

---

*) I had to take this line entirely from the ancient Greek translation <note>The author is referring to the Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> for it to make sound sense. Regarding many other features in this portrait, one should remember that it is the poet speaking, who always applies the strongest colors. This animal often grows between 20 and 30 feet long and perhaps 5 feet thick; in their large scale, they are in body what the garden lizard is in small scale. On their four short feet they have claws; they can run very fast, but they turn slowly and cumbersomely. The head is long, broad at the back, pointed at the front, and covered with large square shields (which in other animals are called scales). The eyes are not very large but are very sharp-sighted. The entire body has 20–24 transverse rows of elongated, square hard shells, or armor plates, which lie atop one another like roof tiles, half-covering each other, and are so hard that he cannot be struck or wounded through them. In the tail, which is often longer than the body and equipped with the same impenetrable shells, they have their particular strength, and they strike everything to the ground with it. They swim in the water so that the head and back protrude, but dive quickly when they want to seize prey. Maliciously, they often lie in the reeds and suddenly spring forth, snatching sheep, cattle, other animals, horses, mules, turtles, large fish, etc. They never chew <term>vertauen: an archaic term here meaning to masticate or grind food; crocodiles typically swallow prey in large chunks.</term> their food; they bite a person only once or twice in half and swallow the mass whole. With the help of their

His equal is not found upon the dry land; he is meant to know no fear. He looks down upon all from on high and is king in the water world. —

### Ch. XLII.

Job then said to God: "Ah, I well understand that you are almighty, and that no undertaking is too difficult for you. Who was the ignorant one who criticized your decrees? I have listened to you with the greatest attention; I have not turned my eye away from you, but I myself disapprove of what I have said; I repent and bow down in dust and ashes." —

# Job Ch. XLII.

When God had spoken all this to Job, God said to Eliphaz the Temanite: "I am displeased with you and your two friends, for you have not judged me as truthfully as my faithful servant Job. Therefore, take seven bulls and seven rams, go to my servant Job, offer them there for yourselves, and let my worshiper Job intercede for you; perhaps for his sake I will not treat you as your lack of wisdom <note>original: "Unverstand," suggesting a failure of insight or judgment.</note> deserves. For you have not always judged my governance of the world as truthfully as my steadfast servant Job." The three men, Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar, did as God had commanded them, and God heard Job’s intercession.

And while Job himself was still praying for his friends, he also received back everything that had been taken from him. God even gave him double everything he had possessed before. All his relatives and old acquaintances came together and ate with him in his house. Everyone had compassion for him and comforted him regarding the misfortune he had endured, and each gave him silver and a gold ring. *)
